hints: Compare the functional groups in each pair, look for two different reactive groups that can join with loss of a small molecule versus a C=C double bond that can open up to join.
walkthrough:
Sort by what joins and what is lost**
Think of it like this. If monomers join by opening a C=C double bond with nothing lost, that is addition. If they join by two different functional groups reacting together with loss of a small molecule like water or HCl, that is condensation.

Apply to the three pairs**
$\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ is a diol and $\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ is a dicarboxylic acid, -OH + -COOH gives ester links + $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, so condensation. The second pair is an acyl dichloride, -COCl, plus a diol, -OH, giving ester links + HCl, so condensation. The third pair, $\text{CH}_3\text{CHCF}_2$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CHCH}_2$, are both alkenes containing C=C, they join by opening the double bond with no small molecule lost, so addition.

Final answer: $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ and $\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$: condensation
terephthaloyl dichloride and $\text{HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-OH}$: condensation
$\text{CH}_3\text{CHCF}_2$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CHCH}_2$: addition

hints: Recall what happens when the $\text{-NH}_2$ group of one 2-aminopropanoic acid meets the $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ group of the next, and what small molecule is lost.
Think how to write the linked residue so the amide link $\text{-CO-NH-}$ is clearly shown with the side chain $\text{-CH}_3$ still on the alpha carbon.
Consider how to show that the chain continues beyond the three units drawn, and how to mark a single repeating block within that longer chain.
walkthrough:
See the monomer as bifunctional**
$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$ has both an amine end and a carboxylic acid end in the same molecule. So one molecule can act as the amine partner and the next as the acid partner. When $\text{-NH}_2$ + $\text{-COOH}$ react, you get an amide link $\text{-CONH-}$ plus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. This is condensation, forming a polypeptide.

Build three residues linked head to tail**
Line them up $\text{N}$ to $\text{C}$ direction each time. Write the chain as: $\text{---NH-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO---NH-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO---NH-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO---}$. Check each alpha carbon still carries $\text{CH}_3$ and H, and each junction is $\text{-CO-NH-}$. Do not add any other monomer, only Ala residues.

Show it is part of a longer polymer**
Put short continuation bonds sticking out at the left N end and the right C=O end to show the chain goes on. Then bracket or circle just one $\text{-NH-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO-}$ block and label it repeat unit. That one block is what repeats to make the whole chain.

Final answer: Polypeptide: $\text{---NH-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO-NH-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO-NH-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO---}$ with amide links shown, three Ala residues only, continuation bonds at both ends, one repeat unit $\text{-NH-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO-}$ clearly bracketed/labelled.

hints: Check the central carbon of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$ and count how many different groups are attached to it.
Recall what type of stereoisomerism occurs when a tetrahedral carbon has four different substituents, and how wedge and hashed bonds show the two non-superimposable mirror images.
walkthrough:
Spot the chiral centre**
Look at carbon 2 in $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH(NH}_2\text{)-CO}_2\text{H}$. It is bonded to four different groups: $\text{-H}$, $\text{-CH}_3$, $\text{-NH}_2$ and $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$. Any tetrahedral carbon with four different groups is chiral, so it can exist as two non-superimposable mirror images.

Draw the mirror pair in 3D**
Draw the central C with normal lines for two groups in the plane, a solid wedge for a bond coming out toward you, and a hashed wedge for a bond going back. For example, isomer 1: $\text{COOH}$ top, $\text{NH}_2$ left, $\text{CH}_3$ on wedge, H on dash. Isomer 2: same but $\text{CH}_3$ and H swapped, so $\text{CH}_3$ on dash and H on wedge. Keep all four groups identical, only the spatial arrangement changes.

Name the relationship**
Because these are mirror images that cannot be superimposed and differ only in the 3D arrangement around a chiral centre, this is optical isomerism. They would rotate plane polarised light in opposite directions.

Final answer: Two tetrahedral 3D structures with central C bonded to $\text{NH}_2$, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$/$\text{COOH}$ and H, one substituent on solid wedge and one on hashed wedge, mirror images with positions of two groups swapped.
Type of stereoisomerism: optical isomerism.

hints: Recall which two-part adhesive uses a diepoxide monomer like W plus a diamine hardener to form a cross-linked network without solvent.
walkthrough:
Recognise W as a diepoxide**
The skeletal formula shows two three-membered epoxide rings joined together. Epoxide rings are highly strained and open easily when attacked by a nucleophile such as an amine. Mixing a diepoxide with a diamine hardener therefore builds a heavily cross-linked thermoset. That two-part, non-solvent-based adhesive is called an epoxy resin.

hints: Think of the simplest alkyl chain that can carry one $\text{-NH}_2$ group at each end so the two amines are on different carbons and both can open epoxide rings.
walkthrough:
Design a molecule with two separate amine ends**
You need an alkyl chain with a primary amine at two different positions so each end can attack and open an epoxide ring to cross-link chains. The simplest example is 1,2-diaminoethane, $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. The two $\text{-NH}_2$ groups are on different carbons, satisfying the definition of a suitable diamine hardener.
Final answer: $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ (any diamine with two $\text{-NH}_2$ groups on different carbons, e.g. $\text{H}_2\text{N(CH}_2\text{)}_n\text{NH}_2$).
